cards.front: What should you know about nanoparticle?
cards.back: A particle that has a size between 1 nm and 100 nm (1 × 10⁻⁹ m to 100 × 10⁻⁹ m). Nanoparticles are typically a few hundred atoms in size.

cards.front: What should you know about nanoscience?
cards.back: The study of structures that are 1-100 nm in size. It involves studying and working with materials on an extremely small scale.

cards.front: What should you know about surface area to volume ratio (sa:v)?
cards.back: The ratio of the surface area of a particle to its volume. As particles get smaller, their surface area to volume ratio increases dramatically.

cards.front: What should you know about 1 nanometre (1 nm) = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m = 0.000000001 m.?
cards.back: A nanoparticle is roughly the same size as a few hundred atoms. Nanoparticles are much smaller than fine particles and coarse particles.

cards.front: What should you know about why sa:v ratio matters?
cards.back: Nanoparticles have a very high surface area to volume ratio compared to bulk materials. This means a much larger fraction of the atoms are on the surface, making nanoparticles much more chemically reactive than the same substance in bulk form. This is why nanoparticle catalysts are very effective.

cards.front: What should you know about risks of nanoparticles?
cards.back: Because nanoparticles are so small, they can be absorbed into the body and into cells. The long-term health effects of exposure to nanoparticles are not fully understood. Nanoparticles could be toxic or cause harm in ways that larger particles of the same substance do not.
Greater than 2500 nm (2.5 μm) (e.g. Dust, pollen, fine sand)
100 nm to 2500 nm (0.1-2.5 μm) (e.g. PM2.5 air pollution particles)
1 nm to 100 nm (e.g. Nanoparticle silver, titanium dioxide nanoparticles)
Nanoparticles can carry drugs to specific cells, reducing side effects and improving effectiveness
Titanium dioxide (TiO₂) nanoparticles block UV light effectively while being colourless on the skin
High SA:V ratio means more surface available for reactions, making nanoparticle catalysts very efficient
Nanoparticles can be used to make smaller, faster and more efficient electronic components
Self-cleaning windows and anti-bacterial coatings use nanoparticles
Nanoparticle sensors can detect very small amounts of substances
